newsitem.title: USA: Miami fears weigh on muni bond insurance stocks.
newsitem.headline: Miami fears weigh on muni bond insurance stocks.

text.p: Shares of municipal bond insurance companies fell again Tuesday in part because investors fear a Miami default, but stock market analysts say the reaction has been overblown.

"I would view it as a buy opportunity," said Caitlin Long, a analyst who covers the industry for Salomon Brothers. Long said that, even in the unlikely event of default, the bond insurers would be on the hook only for relatively small debt service payments.

MBIA Insurance Corp, for example, would be facing an annual payment equivalent to just 0.5 percent of the company's revenues, Long said. MBIA, a unit of MBIA Inc, saw its share price fall as much as 2-1/8 to 96-1/4 in intraday trading, but has since recovered to 97-1/2. The price is down from its Dec 3 all-time high of 103-5/8.

In addition to the relatively small exposure companies like MBIA face, analysts say they also take comfort from the fact that all of the bond insurers maintain separate reserves to pay for unexpected claims.
That means the companies' earnings may not take a hit under even the worst-case default scenario.

Still, the bond insurers' stocks have historically been volatile after news breaks about fiscal problems hitting city or state credits. When Philadelphia teetered on the brink of insolvency in 1990, for example, MBIA's share price fell nearly in half.
But Louise Costikyan, an analyst at Merrill Lynch & Co, said reactions to subsequent municipal market turmoil have gradually moderated as investors grew more comfortable with insurers' actual risks.

"The stocks' reaction has become less volatile in each succeeding event," Costikyan said. She noted that share prices recovered quickly even after the unprecedented bankruptcy filing by Orange County, Calif., in December 1994.

In the Miami situation, insurers' headaches began in late November, when the city said it faced a $68 million budget deficit that totaled nearly 25 percent of its $275 million annual budget. Since then, Fla. Gov Lawton Chiles has stepped in to create an emergency oversight committee to straighten out the city's finances.
"I think within the week we'll probably have flushed out these Miami developments" with regard to their effects on the insurers' share prices, Costikyan said.
Defaults in the $1.3 trillion muni market are extremely rare, and insurers only guarantee in such cases that they will pay principal and interest as they come due, not all at once.
So while MBIA has insured a total of $25.3 million of Miami general obligation bonds, the average annual debt service the company said it is responsible for is $2.1 million.
MBIA also insured $65.7 million of Miami revenue bonds, but they are not dependent on the city's ailing general fund and would be at risk only if the situation worsens considerably, analysts said.

Shares of AMBAC Inc, which insures municipal bonds through its AMBAC Indemnity Corp unit, fell 1/8 Tuesday to 65-1/4. The shares were as low as 64-1/4 Tuesday, compared to a Dec 3 all-time high of 69.
Financial Guaranty Insurance Co, which is not publicly traded, has the largest exposure to Miami.

The firm said it insured $116.5 million of GO bonds and $82.7 million in so-called "non ad-valorem" debt backed by special city fees. The combined annual debt service exposure on that guarantee is $15.4 million. FGIC is a unit of GE Capital Services, a subsidiary of General Electric Co.

Financial Security Assurance, a unit of Financial Security Assurance Holdings Ltd, said it has no exposure to Miami. FSA was up 3/8 at 31-7/8, but analysts said the gains are not likely related to the firm having escaped the Miami crisis. FSA shares are traded extremely thinly, so single transactions can affect share prices dramatically.
For their part, executives at the companies that are facing Miami risk take pains to educate equity investors on the nature of their exposure.
All of the major insurers in recent days have issued statements about the Miami situation, stressing that they are working closely with state and city officials to ensure that no default occurs.
Equity analysts also stressed that the recent deterioration in bond insurance stocks is not entirely Miami's fault.

Robert Ryan, a Lehman Brothers analyst, said it is most likely a mix of factors that include Miami's troubles, the general rise in overall interest rates recently, and deterioration in stock prices in general.
